title: Centesimus Annus (1991)
hook: after communism falls: markets have value but also limits

segments.voice: Yesterday, structures of sin: harm built into how things are set up, rooted in human choices. Your line was sin in systems. Who did you tell about the system you noticed? Day one thousand three hundred nine.

A price tag. Some things wear one easily: a loaf of bread, a used car, an hour of a plumber's time. Other things turn strange the moment someone tries to stick one on: a friendship, a vote, a child. John Paul the Second wrote a letter marking a hundred years since Rerum Novarum, after the communist governments of Eastern Europe had fallen. It could have handed down a simple verdict on which economic system had won. Instead it gives something more careful: the market is a real good, and the market has edges. Its name means the hundredth year. Today's word is Centesimus Annus.
screen: `SOME THINGS WEAR A PRICE TAG.` → `SOME THINGS NEVER SHOULD.` → `THE HUNDREDTH YEAR.`

segments.voice: First, what markets do well. The letter calls the free market an efficient way to use resources and meet needs. It praises initiative, enterprise and work, and says profit has a proper place as a sign that a business is doing its job. That's not grudging. It's real respect. Second, where markets stop. The same letter says there are many human needs the market can't meet, because the people who have them have nothing to pay with. And it goes further: some goods, by their very nature, cannot and must not be bought or sold. It leaves the list open; a verdict in court might be one, a child's care another. Profit is a sign, the letter adds, but not the only sign. A business is first a community of people. Third, having and being. The letter warns about consumerism: not the wish to live better, which it calls good, but a way of life aimed at having more rather than being more. Jesus puts it bluntly in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "a man's life doth not consist in the abundance of things which he possesseth." Fourth, the big question. Is a free economy the answer, then? The letter's reply is careful. If it means freedom to work and do business, set inside a strong framework of law that serves the whole human person, yes. If it means an economy answerable to nothing but itself, no. A market inside a moral frame, the letter says, not a market as the frame.
screen: `WHAT MARKETS DO WELL.` · `GOODS THAT MUST NOT BE BOUGHT.` · `HAVING MORE, OR BEING MORE.` · then, large: `NOT IN THE ABUNDANCE OF THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: buy one thing thoughtfully. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the next thing you're likely to buy: groceries, a gift, something in a cart you haven't checked out. Hold it in your mind. Who made it, and were they paid fairly? Do you need it, or does it promise to make you more than you are? Is there a way to buy it that serves people better? No guilt needed, just attention. If you pray, you can ask for a free heart toward things. If you don't, simply decide what you'll do. The bell holds the time.

Centesimus Annus. The hundredth year: markets have value, and limits. This week: read the signs, development is peace, with the poor, justice is gospel, the person first, sin in systems, markets have limits. Today's word.
Your line: markets have limits. Today, make the one purchase you thought about with your eyes open, and notice one good in your life that no money could buy. Day one thousand three hundred nine.

howItsDone: Catholics draw on Centesimus Annus in business ethics, economics courses at Catholic universities and in thinking about consumer choices, and it is often read together with Rerum Novarum.
